meta.title: Bible App vs Olive Tree: Daily Reading or Deep Study? (2026)
meta.description: Bible App vs Olive Tree on iPhone, compared: price, offline reading, study tools and App Store sizes, plus how to keep your chosen verses on the lock screen.

sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: Put **FaithWall** on your lock screen whichever reader you choose, then settle **Bible App vs Olive Tree** by how you read: YouVersion's Bible App wins for free, plan-driven daily reading, and Olive Tree wins for offline study with commentaries and Greek and Hebrew tools. The lock-screen layer is free to download and sets up in about a minute.

**FaithWall** is our app, so weigh this page knowing that. It isn't a Bible reader and doesn't compete with either one. It shows the verses you choose on your iPhone lock screen, as a wallpaper applied by an Apple Shortcut or a widget that rotates them. That's the honest case for adding it to whichever app wins below.

sections.text: If you're weighing the **Bible App vs Olive Tree**, you're choosing between two ideas of what a Bible app is for. YouVersion's Bible App is built to get you reading every day: plans, friends, verse images. Olive Tree is built to help you understand what you read: commentary that follows your place in the text, parallel translations, original-language tools. Both are free to download, both rate 4.8 or higher on the App Store, and both shipped an update in the first week of October 2026. Neither keeps the verses you chose in view once it's closed, which is where FaithWall fits.

"The Bible App" almost always means YouVersion, published by Life.Church and listed on the App Store simply as "Bible". The confusion is fair: Olive Tree's own listing is titled "Bible App - Read & Study Daily" and is sold by Gospel Technologies LLC, so check the publisher line before you tap Get. For YouVersion against a lock-screen app instead of a study app, see [our YouVersion head-to-head](/blog/faithwall-vs-bible-app).
Bible App vs Olive Tree at a glance

Every figure below comes from each app's US App Store listing, checked October 13, 2026. Sizes and versions change with each update, so treat this as a dated snapshot. Prayer and devotional apps get the same treatment in our [side-by-side guide to Christian iPhone apps](/christian-app-comparisons).

| | YouVersion Bible App | Olive Tree |
|---|---|---|
| App Store seller | Life.Church | Gospel Technologies LLC |
| Price | Free, no in-app purchases | Free download; resources and study packs sold in-app |
| Bible versions | 3,500+ in 2,300+ languages | Free major translations incl. ESV, NIV, KJV, NKJV, CSB; others sold in-app |
| Offline | Select versions only | Bibles and study resources download in full |
| Audio Bibles | Select versions; can't be downloaded | Narrated or dramatized, in popular translations |
| Study tools | Notes, highlights, plans, videos | Study Center, Resource Guide, cross-references, Greek and Hebrew tools |
| Download size | 181.2 MB | 119.9 MB |
| Requires | iOS 18.0 or later | iOS 17.0 or later |
| Latest version | 11.33.1 (Oct 6, 2026) | 8.1.3 (Oct 7, 2026) |
| App Store rating | 4.9 from about 14M ratings | 4.8 from about 324K ratings |

sections.description: Per Life.Church's App Store listing, checked October 13, 2026. Olive Tree's listing claims more than 8 million, about one install for every 90 of YouVersion's.

sections.text: Where the Bible App wins: reading every day

YouVersion wins whenever the goal is simply to keep reading. It costs nothing and sells nothing (its App Store page has no in-app purchases section), and it pairs thousands of reading plans with a Friends feed showing what people you trust highlight and note. A free account syncs notes, highlights and plans across devices. The trade-offs are on its own listing: offline reading covers select versions only, and audio Bibles can't be downloaded, so a flight can cut you off mid-chapter. It also needs iOS 18 or later.
Where Olive Tree wins: studying what you read

Olive Tree wins as soon as you want to know what a passage means, not just what it says. Its Study Center follows your place in the text and surfaces matching commentary and study notes from your library, with no searching. Version 8.1.3, released October 7, added Compare: tap a verse number to see it across every translation you've installed, up to five verses at a time. Its listing says everything downloads for offline study, and your library syncs across iPhone, iPad and Mac.

The depth costs money past the free translations. The App Store lists a Starter Pack at $2.99 a month, an ESV Study Pack at $5.99 a month and the ESV Study Bible at $47.99 once. The interface comes in four languages; YouVersion's comes in dozens.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

items: **Daily plan and accountability:** the Bible App. Plans and a Friends feed beat any study tool for showing up.
**Leading a group or teaching:** Olive Tree, with commentary that tracks the passage you're on.
**Planes or bad signal:** Olive Tree, whose Bibles and resources download in full.
**Never want to see a price tag:** the Bible App, with no in-app purchases.
**Want both:** run both. Read in one, study in the other.

sections.content: Neither app keeps the verses you're actually working on in front of you. **FaithWall** shows the verses you choose on your lock screen, as a wallpaper an Apple Shortcut applies or a widget that rotates them every hour, 8 hours or day, so what you read or studied stays in view between sessions.

sections.text: If that's the piece you're missing, here are [the apps that put Bible verses on your lock screen, ranked](/best-bible-verse-lock-screen-apps).

The usual workaround is making one of these apps cover the lock screen too. YouVersion's Verse Images feature turns a verse into shareable art, so people save one and set it as their wallpaper. That holds until the passage you're reading moves on. Then the image goes stale, and swapping wallpapers by hand is the first habit to die. YouVersion's Verse of the Day widget shows its pick for the day, not your passage, and Olive Tree's help center describes its Verse of the Day as an in-app screen plus an optional notification. Either way, what you studied stays in the app until you open it again.
That's the gap FaithWall closes: you pick the verses, from this week's plan or last night's study passage, and they rotate on the lock screen on their own.

sections.content: Studying a passage in Olive Tree this week? Save the two or three verses at its center and put those on your lock screen instead of a random verse of the day. Seeing the passage you studied all week is what moves it into memory.

sections.text: Our call: start with the Bible App unless you already know you want commentaries. It costs nothing, never upsells, and its plans fix the problem most people actually have, which is opening a Bible at all. Add Olive Tree the first time you finish a chapter with questions the text can't answer. That's where the **Bible App vs Olive Tree** question stops being either/or.

Want more study depth? Our [Bible study app comparison](/blog/best-bible-study-app-iphone-2026) sets Blue Letter Bible and Logos beside Olive Tree, and the [best Christian apps for iPhone](/blog/best-christian-app-for-iphone-2026) covers prayer and devotional apps too.
